html:
Five rules that govern every lift

  1. The bar stays over midfoot. The system (you + bar) is balanced when the combined centre of mass sits over the middle of the foot. With heavy loads the bar dominates, so in squat and deadlift the bar path is a near-vertical line over midfoot when viewed from the side. Any horizontal drift is wasted work and a balance correction you pay for in strength.
  2. Moment arms decide which muscles work. The horizontal distance from a joint to the bar's line of action sets the torque that joint must produce. Hips far behind the bar load hip extensors; knees far in front of the bar load the quads. Technique choices mostly move load between these two.
  3. Rigid trunk, then move. Force made by the legs only reaches the bar if the torso doesn't bend. Intra-abdominal pressure (the brace) is what turns the torso into a stiff column.
  4. Shortest legal range of motion, in the strongest legal position. Grip width, stance, arch and bar position are chosen to cut distance and keep leverage, within the rules.
  5. Same rep every time. Technique is a skill. Reps at 70% should look exactly like reps at 95%. Submaximal volume is where the pattern is built; heavy singles test it.
Shared by all three lifts

The brace

The brace is the part of technique that transfers between all three lifts, and the one most lifters underrate. Done properly, the abdominal wall, obliques, spinal erectors, diaphragm and pelvic floor co-contract around a pressurised cavity. The belt gives the abdominal wall something to push against; it does not do the work for you.

Bracing sequence

  1. Set the ribcage down over the pelvis first. Flared ribs make the cylinder short and leaky.
  2. Breathe low, through the nose or mouth, into the belt. Feel the belt tighten at the sides and back, not only the front. Shoulders should not rise.
  3. Hold the air (Valsalva) and tense around it, as if about to take a punch to the stomach. Aim near maximal for heavy singles, roughly 70–80% effort on lighter sets.
  4. Keep it through the sticking point. Exhale only near lockout or between reps. Many lifters re-breathe at the top of each rep on squats and deadlifts; on bench, one breath per 1–3 reps is common.

Belt fit

  • Tight enough that you need a full breath to fill it, loose enough to take that breath. Usually you can slide flat fingers in when relaxed.
  • Squat: belt sits over the navel area. Deadlift: often one notch looser and a little higher, so it doesn't jam the thighs in the start position.
  • Train most technique work without a belt too, so the brace is yours and not the belt's.

If you have high blood pressure or cardiovascular issues, check with a doctor before using heavy Valsalva bracing.

Personalise

Your build

Grip width, stance, bar position and pulling style should come from your body, not from a lifter you watched online. Enter what you can measure. Anything you leave blank is estimated from your height with standard body proportions. Every number below updates as you type, the live models in each lift section load your body, and each lift section gets a short summary of your setup. Values are saved in this browser only.

Measurements

cm
Barefoot.
cm
Back to a wall, arms straight out to the sides, fingertip to fingertip.
cm
Bony tip to bony tip of the shoulders (acromion), measured across the back by a partner. Not the widest point of the delts.
cm
Standing: bony bump at the side of the hip (greater trochanter) to the joint line on the outside of the knee.
cm
Sit on a hard flat surface, back and head against a wall: surface to top of head. Used for torso length.
cm
Half-kneel facing a wall, front heel down. Move the foot back until the knee only just touches the wall. Toe-to-wall distance, worse side.

Mobility & feel

On hands and knees, rock your hips back toward your heels with the knees at different widths. The width where you sink deepest without the low back rounding is your hips' natural squat width.
A raised heel adds roughly 6–10° of usable shin angle.

Where you miss

Your segments

Squat: your torso lean by stance and bar position

Bottom position at just-below-parallel, using your segments and usable knee travel. Wider stances shorten the femur as seen from the side, which lets you sit more upright. Lower lean = more upright. The highlighted cell is your recommended setup.

These are starting points calculated from a simplified model, not a final answer. Test the recommendation for 3–4 weeks at moderate loads, film it, and adjust by feel. If something hurts, that overrides any number on this page.

Squat

The squat is a knee and hip movement in which the torso angle is an output, not a choice. Bar position, femur length and ankle mobility set the torso angle that keeps the bar over midfoot. Low bar puts more work on the hips and allows a more forward lean; high bar is more upright and more quad-dominant. Most powerlifters squat low bar or a "mid bar" compromise.

Setup & walkout

  1. Rack height: bar at mid-sternum to armpit level so you unrack with a quarter-inch of knee bend, not a calf raise.
  2. Grip: as narrow as your shoulders allow while keeping wrists straight. Low bar: thumbs over or under, wrist neutral, bar sits in the hand and is pinned by the back, not supported by the wrists. Elbows point back and down, not straight up.
  3. Bar placement: high bar on the upper traps; low bar just below the spine of the scapula on the rear delts, which you create by squeezing the upper back. Centre it: check the knurling distance on both sides.
  4. Get under it with feet under the bar, squeeze the shoulder blades, brace, and stand up with both legs. Never unrack from a split stance.
  5. Walkout in 3 steps: one back, one back to width, one optional adjustment. Long walkouts burn energy and invite foot errors.
  6. Stance: typically heels around shoulder width, toes out 15–30°. Wider for low bar or long femurs, narrower for high bar. Find it by testing a bodyweight squat where your hips drop between your heels with no pelvic tuck.
  7. Breathe and brace at the top, then wait for the command (in meets: "Squat").

Descent, bottom, drive

  • Break at hips and knees together. Knees track over toes (slightly out). Hips go back and down. Leading hard with the hips ("sit back") collapses the knees forward late and wrecks bar path.
  • Controlled speed. Fast enough to use the stretch reflex, slow enough to hit the same depth every rep. About 1–1.5 s down at heavy loads.
  • Foot pressure: tripod: big toe, little toe, heel. Weight stays midfoot. If the heels or toes lift, the bar has left midfoot.
  • Bottom: hit depth by a few centimetres. Keep tension, don't relax into the hole. A slight posterior pelvic tilt at the very bottom (butt wink) is normal for many people and only matters if it becomes a big flex under load.
  • Drive the upper back into the bar and the floor away. Chest and hips rise at the same rate: the torso angle should stay the same in the first half of the ascent.
  • Lockout: squeeze glutes, stand tall, knees locked. Wait for "Rack".

Cues that work

Spread the floorActivates hip external rotators, keeps knees tracking over toes.
Chest up into the barOn ascent. Stops hips shooting up first.
Bend the bar over your backUpper-back tightness on low bar, protects the elbows.
Sit between your heelsHips drop down between the feet rather than far back.
Grip the floorTripod foot, stable arch.
Push up through the trapsLead the ascent with the back, not the hips.

Faults → cause → fix

What you seeLikely causeFix
Hips shoot up first out of the hole ("squat morning")Quads weaker than hips; loss of upper-back tension; descending too fast and bouncingCue "chest up into the bar"; pause squats (2–3 s); high-bar or SSB squats; leg press/hack squat volume
Knees cave in (valgus) on the way upAdductor-dominant drive, fatigue, stance too wide or toes too straight"Spread the floor"; slightly more toe-out; tempo squats; a small valgus that self-corrects is common at max and not always a problem
Bar drifts forward, weight onto toesHips too far back at the start, upper back rounds, or knees stay back then shoot forwardBreak hips and knees together; tighten upper back; film from the side and check bar over midfoot
Inconsistent depthUnknown "feel" of depth; speed changes rep to repBox squat to a legal-height target occasionally; pause squats; film every top set
Elbow / wrist pain on low barBar supported by hands, grip too narrow for shoulder mobility, wrists bent backWiden grip; neutral wrist with thumbs over; drive upper back into bar; consider mid-bar
Losing brace at bottom (big pelvic tuck, chest drops)Brace released in descent; depth beyond current mobilityRe-brace before each rep; tempo squats; train just past legal depth, not ass-to-grass

Sticking points & variants

Where you failVariant / accessory
Out of the holePause squat (2–3 s), pin squat from bottom, tempo squat (eccentric emphasis), front squat
Mid-range, hips riseSSB or high-bar squat, pause squat, belt squat, Bulgarian split squat
LockoutRarely a true sticking point. Usually a bar path or brace problem earlier. Check video.

Competition rules (IPF-style)

SQUAT
Given once you are upright, knees locked, bar settled. Starting early = red light.
DEPTH
Top surface of the legs at the hip joint must be lower than the top of the knees.
NO DOUBLE BOUNCE
Any downward movement of the bar during the ascent is a fail.
RACK
Wait for the command after lockout. Feet must not move (heel/toe rises and stepping are faults).

Rules differ slightly by federation. Check the current technical rulebook for yours before a meet.

Bench press

The powerlifting bench is a full-body lift. The legs push you toward the head end of the bench, the upper back is the platform, the arch shortens range of motion, and the chest and triceps move the bar on a slightly diagonal J-shaped path. The shoulder blades stay retracted and depressed for the whole set.

Setup

  1. Eyes under the bar as you lie down, so the unrack is a short arc, not a long reach.
  2. Retract and depress the shoulder blades: pinch them together and drive them down toward your back pockets. Many lifters grab the bar, pull themselves up, set the scapulae, then lower onto the upper traps.
  3. Grip: start where forearms are vertical at the bottom (front view). Bar in the heel of the palm, over the forearm bones, wrist slightly extended but stacked. Full grip with the thumb around; thumbless is banned in most federations.
  4. Feet: plant them and push. Feet back under the knees for a big arch, or further forward for a flatter, more stable setup. Heels down or up depends on federation rules and preference.
  5. Build the arch from the upper back: chest up toward the bar, glutes stay on the bench. The arch comes from the thoracic spine and hips, not just the low back.
  6. Unrack with a spotter or a straight-arm pull, bring the bar over the shoulders, re-tighten the lats, breathe and brace.

The press

  • Lower with the lats. "Pull the bar to your chest" or "bend the bar": lats engaged, elbows tucked to roughly 45–70° from the torso at the bottom.
  • Touch point: lower sternum / bottom of the pecs. Same spot every rep. In competition, hold motionless until "Press".
  • Drive with legs as you press. Leg drive pushes you up the bench, not your hips up. Butt stays in contact.
  • Elbows flare progressively as the bar travels back over the shoulders. Bar back toward the face, elbows under it.
  • Lock out over the shoulder joints, hold for "Rack".
  • Shoulders stay pinned. If the shoulders roll forward off the bench at lockout, the setup is lost and the next rep will be weaker.

Cues that work

Bend the barLats and external rotation on the descent.
Push yourself away from the barUpper back drives into the bench instead of arms pushing up.
Back to the rackBar path toward the face after the chest.
Slide up the benchLeg drive that doesn't lift the hips.
Shoulders in your back pocketsScapular depression; keeps the arch.
Squeeze the bar offTension from the pause, no relax before the press.

Faults → cause → fix

What you seeLikely causeFix
Bar presses straight up and stalls in front of the shouldersNo path back toward the face; elbows stay tucked too longCue "back to the rack"; flare the elbows as the bar leaves the chest; video from the side
Butt leaves the benchLeg drive aimed upward; feet too far back with heels downPush horizontally toward the head; feet slightly forward; pause bench with conscious hip contact
Shoulders roll forward at lockoutScapulae not kept retracted; pressing "through" the bar at the topLock out by pushing yourself into the bench; re-set between reps; lighter tempo work
Bar sinks or bounces at the touchLosing lat tension at the bottom, relaxing in the pauseLong-pause bench (3 s); Spoto press; "squeeze the bar off"
Uneven lockoutGrip not centred, one side weaker, scapulae asymmetricalCheck knurling marks; DB press volume; film from the head end
Wrist painBar too high in the palm, wrist bent backBar into the heel of the palm; wrist wraps for heavy sets

Sticking points & variants

Where you failVariant / accessory
Off the chestLong-pause bench, Spoto press (stop 2–3 cm above chest), wider grip bench, DB press, feet-up bench for upper-body-only control
Mid-range (~5–10 cm up)Pin press at the sticking height, Larsen press, tempo bench (eccentric emphasis)
LockoutClose-grip bench, board press, JM press, triceps volume (dips, overhead extensions)

Competition rules (IPF-style)

CONTACT
Head, shoulders and buttocks on the bench; feet in solid contact with the floor. Whether heels must be down varies by federation.
START
Given once the bar is held at arm's length and motionless.
PRESS
After the bar is lowered to the chest/abdomen and is visibly motionless. No heave, no sinking into the chest after the command.
RACK
Given after even lockout. Downward movement of the bar during the press is a fail.
GRIP
Max 81 cm between index fingers; thumbs around the bar.

Deadlift

The deadlift starts from a dead stop, so the setup decides most of the outcome. The arms are vertical ropes; the shoulders sit just in front of the bar; the hip height is whatever your limbs dictate once those two constraints are satisfied. Conventional puts more demand on the back and hips; sumo shortens the range and moves work to the quads and adductors. Neither is "cheating"; pick the one your build favours.

Setup: the 5-step pull

  1. Stance: conventional, feet about hip width (where you'd jump from), toes slightly out; sumo, shins near the plates or a bit inside, toes out 30–45°. Bar over midfoot, roughly 2–3 cm from the shins.
  2. Grip: bend at the hips with straight-ish legs and grip just outside the legs (conventional) or shoulder width (sumo). Hook grip or mixed grip for heavy sets; straps are fine in training but not in competition.
  3. Shins to the bar: bend the knees until the shins touch the bar. Don't move the bar.
  4. Chest up, lats on: "squeeze oranges in your armpits". The back sets to neutral and the hips rise to their natural height. Don't squat the deadlift with hips too low.
  5. Brace and take the slack out: pull until the bar clicks against the plates, body tight, then push the floor away. Some lifters wedge into the bar from a higher position (common in sumo); others use a quick dynamic start. Both work if the position is the same at lift-off.

The pull

  • Legs first, back holds angle. Off the floor, the torso angle stays nearly constant until the bar passes the knees.
  • Bar drags the legs. It stays in contact with the shins and thighs. Any gap is a longer moment arm.
  • Hips through at the knees. Once the bar clears the knees, drive the hips forward to the bar.
  • Lockout: stand tall, knees and hips locked, shoulders back. No hyperextension lean, no shrug needed.
  • Lower under control on the "Down" command, hands on the bar until it's on the floor.

Cues that work

Push the floor awayLeg-driven start instead of pulling with the back.
Protect your armpitsLats on, bar stays close.
Pull the slack outBar clicks before it leaves the floor.
Chest up, hips stayStops hips rising first.
Hips to the barLockout, without leaning back.
Spread the floorSumo: knees out over toes, hips close to bar.

Faults → cause → fix

What you seeLikely causeFix
Hips shoot up first, becomes a stiff-leg pullHips set too low (squatting the pull), weak quads, no slack pulled outLet the hips set where the model says; pull the slack; paused deadlift 2–3 cm off the floor; deficit pulls
Bar drifts forward off the shinsLats loose; shoulders too far behind the bar; bar started too far from the shins"Protect the armpits"; start bar over midfoot; RDLs and lat work
Lower back rounds off the floorBrace lost, position too far from the bar, load beyond current position strengthRe-brace before the slack pull; pause deadlifts; reduce load and own the position
Hitching at lockoutWeak hip extension, bar resting on thighs, slow at the kneeBlock pulls, hip thrusts, RDLs; hitching is a fail in competition
Sumo: can't break the floorHips too far from the bar, knees not out, not wedgedWedge harder, "spread the floor", deficit sumo, paused sumo at the floor
Grip failsInsufficient grip training, chalk, hand position too far in the fingersHook grip practice; heavy holds; bar closer to the base of the fingers

Sticking points & variants

Where you failVariant / accessory
Off the floorDeficit deadlift (2–5 cm), pause just off the floor, front squat or leg press for quads; sumo: deficit sumo, paused wedge
At the kneesPaused deadlift below the knee, tempo deadlift (slow eccentric), RDL, good morning
LockoutBlock pull, banded deadlift, hip thrust, heavy shrugs/holds for upper-back

Competition rules (IPF-style)

NO START CMD
You lift when ready. The bar must not stop on the way up.
LOCKOUT
Knees fully locked, shoulders back, standing erect.
NO HITCH
Supporting the bar on the thighs during the pull (ramping it up) is a fail.
DOWN
Lower with control, hands on the bar until it's on the platform. Dropping it is a fail.
Making it stick

Self-coaching

Filming

  • Squat & deadlift: side view at hip height, perpendicular to the bar. The bar path is only readable from here.
  • Bench: from the side for path, from behind the head for symmetry.
  • A 45° front view shows knee tracking and depth in the squat.
  • Use a bar-path app on top sets to compare weeks.

Using tempo & pauses

  • Slow eccentrics (4–6 s) expose where position is lost; the rep shows the fault in slow motion.
  • Pauses at the hardest point (bottom of the squat, chest on bench, just off the floor on deadlift) build position strength exactly where you miss.
  • Pauses remove the stretch reflex, so loads drop a lot more than with tempo alone.

One fix at a time

  • Pick the single fault that costs the most kg. Give it one external cue for 3–4 weeks.
  • Practise it at 60–80% where you can actually control it. A new cue at 95% rarely holds.
  • Don't chase a position the model or your mobility says you can't reach. A long-femured lifter with a 50° torso lean is doing it right.
